settings.headline: I tried everything for my dry eyes. Then I made the thing that finally fit my life.
settings.author: Thomas Cage
settings.lead: I'm not a doctor. I'm just someone who spent two years with gritty, tired eyes and a bathroom drawer full of things that didn't quite work — and got fed up enough to build something better.
settings.intro_body: If you've been through the same cycle — drops that fade in an hour, warm flannels that go cold in ninety seconds, advice you never manage to keep up — I want to tell you how I got out of it, because the fix turned out to be simpler and less glamorous than I expected.
settings.s1_title: Everything I tried worked for about an hour
settings.s1_body:
Drops first, obviously. Bottle after bottle. They'd soothe things for a while and then I'd be right back to that sandpaper feeling by mid-afternoon. An optometrist eventually explained why: the drops were topping up the watery part of my tears, but the layer that had actually broken down was the oily one that stops tears evaporating. More water, missing lid on the jar.

The fix she suggested was a warm compress. Simple. Cheap. And I could not stick to it — a hot wet flannel is annoying, it cools in seconds, and it drips down your wrists. So I did it twice and gave up, like most people do.
settings.pullquote: The science wasn't the problem. The keeping-it-up was. Nothing I owned made the one thing that helped easy enough to actually do.
settings.s2_title: So I made the version I wished existed
settings.s2_body: I wanted something that held a steady, comfortable warmth long enough to matter, that I'd actually look forward to, and that fit into the ten minutes before bed without any fuss. That's all Dewy is. It's not a miracle and I'll never pretend it is — it's the warm-compress step the eye specialists already recommend, made into something you'll genuinely keep doing.
settings.mech_intro: No mystery ingredients, no big promises. Just the sensible first step, done properly:
settings.mech1_body: Research indicates the eyelid needs to reach around 40°C to soften the thickened oils in the glands. Dewy holds a comfortable, even warmth across the whole lid — the thing a flannel can't do.
settings.mech2_body: The whole reason I built it. Ten minutes, no mess, no dripping — a routine you'll actually repeat, which is the only thing that works.
settings.mech3_body: Washable, comfortable, and calming enough to become the nice part of your evening instead of a chore.
settings.mech4_body: Keep whatever your optometrist gave you. Dewy handles the oil-layer step alongside it — I still use my drops too.
settings.signoff_body: That's the honest story. If your eyes have been quietly wearing you down and nothing's stuck, I think Dewy is worth ten minutes of your evening. And if it isn't for you, you've got 30 days to send it back — no hard feelings.
settings.evidence_title: The part I want to be straight about
settings.evidence_body: Dewy is not a cure and not a replacement for anything your optometrist has given you. What's true is that warm-compress therapy is recognised as a first-line approach for evaporative dry eye and meibomian gland dysfunction in the international TFOS DEWS II consensus, and recommended by major eye-care bodies including the American Optometric Association and American Academy of Ophthalmology. It's one of the simplest, best-evidenced first steps you can take at home — used alongside professional care. That's exactly what I built Dewy to make easy.
